idiom_name: withFrameMillis inside a LaunchedEffect driven by MonotonicFrameClock
implementation_notes: In Compose the frame clock is part of the runtime: MonotonicFrameClock 'provides a time source for display frames and the ability to perform an action on the next frame', and the withFrameMillis clock API runs its lambda with the frame time each frame, suspending the coroutine until the next frame. What replaces the classic structure: the composition's frame clock and the coroutine's cancellation replace the hand-written driver loop and the quit flag; accumulate frame-time deltas inside the lambda and step a fixed dt, exactly as with requestAnimationFrame. On Android the clock is driven by the Choreographer; for plain JVM Kotlin (no Compose) use the coroutine delay loop or a manual nanoTime loop, and when a game framework owns the loop, use its update callback.
pitfalls: withFrameMillis suspends until the next frame, so it yields the frame time, not a fixed period; blocking work inside the lambda stalls the frame and defeats the clock.
The frame clock runs on the composition's dispatcher (the Android main thread): I/O or long math there freezes the UI - move work to another dispatcher and hand results back.
Catching CancellationException or swallowing it breaks structured cancellation and the loop may never stop; let isActive and cancellation propagate.
Compose frame time is a Long in milliseconds; mixing it with System.nanoTime() or kotlin.time values silently mixes units.

variants.name: Hand-written coroutine loop with kotlinx.coroutines delay
variants.implementation_notes: Outside a frame clock, the idiomatic Kotlin driver is a coroutine loop whose suspension is delay: it 'delays coroutine for at least the given time without blocking a thread and resumes it after a specified time', is cancellable, and carries a prompt cancellation guarantee. What replaces the classic structure: the coroutine and its Job replace the thread and the quit flag; delay is at-least timing, so a drift-free loop keeps a deadline (next += period) and delays until it, with a monotonic source (System.nanoTime or kotlin.time.TimeSource) measuring how far behind the loop is. Use this for headless simulations, server ticks and tooling; use a frame clock when a UI owns the cadence.
pitfalls: delay is at-least timing: a busy dispatcher or a long step pushes every later wake-up, so delay from a moving deadline (next += period) instead of delay(period) from now, and log when the loop falls behind.
delay throws CancellationException on cancellation; catching it without rethrowing breaks structured concurrency and skips the loop's cleanup.
A CPU-heavy non-suspending step blocks the dispatcher thread it runs on: dispatch it to the right dispatcher or the loop starves other coroutines.
A manually created CoroutineScope without a parent leaks; tie the scope to the owning component (viewModelScope, service scope) so the loop actually stops.
